Random Planted Forest

Source: R/rpf.R
rpf.Rd

Fits a random planted forest (Hiabu, Mammen and Meyer, 2020) for regression or classification. The model is a sum of trees that each split on at most max_interaction predictors, so it decomposes into main effects and interaction components; see predict_components().

Usage

rpf(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'formula'
rpf(
  formula,
  data,
  max_interaction = 2,
  ntrees = 50,
  splits = 30,
  split_structure = "leaves",
  split_try = 10,
  t_try = 0.4,
  max_candidates = 50,
  split_decay_rate = 0.1,
  delete_leaves = TRUE,
  min_leaf_rows = 1,
  interaction_constraints = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  delta = 0.001,
  epsilon = 0.1,
  purify = FALSE,
  nthreads = 1,
  export_forest = FALSE,
  deterministic = FALSE,
  keep_level_order = FALSE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'data.frame'
rpf(
  x,
  y,
  max_interaction = 2,
  ntrees = 50,
  splits = 30,
  split_structure = "leaves",
  split_try = 10,
  t_try = 0.4,
  max_candidates = 50,
  split_decay_rate = 0.1,

)

Arguments

x, y

[data.frame | matrix | recipe], [numeric | factor]: Predictors and outcome for the x/y interface. x holds the predictors, or is a recipe (then supply data instead of y). The predictors need unique names that do not contain :, which joins predictor names in component names such as x1:x2. y is the outcome vector: numeric for regression, factor for classification. A numeric outcome must be finite. A factor outcome needs at least two classes; levels that do not occur are dropped with a warning.

...

Not currently used, but required for extensibility. Unknown (e.g. misspelled) arguments are an error.

formula

[formula]: A formula with the outcome on the left-hand side and the predictors on the right-hand side, e.g. y ~ x1 + x2. Interaction terms such as x1:x2 or x1 * x2 are an error: they would add a predictor named x1:x2, and : is how components are named. The forest finds interactions itself, up to max_interaction, so list the predictors as y ~ x1 + x2. To fit a product as a predictor of its own, write I(x1 * x2), or add it to data as a column with its own name. Transformed terms of one predictor, such as log(x1), are allowed.

data

[data.frame]: Data containing the predictors and the outcome, used with formula or a recipe x.

max_interaction

[integer(1): 2]: Maximum number of predictors a single tree may split on. 1 fits main effects only (an additive model), 2 adds pairwise interactions, and so on. 0 uses all predictors and values above the number of predictors are reduced to it.

ntrees

[integer(1): 50]: Number of tree families, i.e. the size of the forest. Each family is grown on a bootstrap sample and predictions are averaged.

splits

[integer(1): 30]: Number of split rounds per tree family. The main tuning parameter: more splits fit more complex functions. A round splits the best of its candidates; near saturation, when every candidate's leaf is too small to split, a round can make no split.

split_structure

[character(1): "leaves"]: How split candidates are formed and sampled; one of "leaves", "hist", "cur_trees_1", "cur_trees_2", or "res_trees". See Details.

split_try

[integer(1): 10]: Number of thresholds evaluated per split candidate.

t_try

[numeric(1): 0.4]: Proportion in (0, 1] of all possible splits sampled as candidates in each round, capped at max_candidates.

max_candidates

[integer(1): 50]: Maximum number of split candidates per round.

split_decay_rate

[numeric(1): 0.1]: Down-weights possible splits that were sampled as candidates but not chosen. Each such round ages a split by one, choosing it resets its age to zero, and splits are sampled with weight exp(-split_decay_rate * age). 0 samples uniformly.

delete_leaves

[logical(1): TRUE]: Whether to delete a parent leaf when splitting along an existing dimension.

min_leaf_rows

[integer(1): 1]: Minimum number of rows of the bootstrap sample on each side of every split, so in every leaf. Leaves without a threshold that keeps this many rows on each side are not drawn as split candidates. Only for regression with split_structure = "leaves"; 1 (no limit) otherwise.

interaction_constraints

[list | NULL: NULL]: Feature sets that restrict which interactions the forest may form, e.g. list(c("x1", "x2"), c("x3", "x4")). Each set is given by predictor names or by column indices: with x, the columns of x; with a formula, the predictors in the order the formula names them (y ~ .: the order of the columns of data); with a recipe, names only (its steps decide the columns). A tree on the predictors T is grown only if T is a subset of one of the sets, as with xgboost's interaction constraints. The subsets of a set stay allowed, so the forest keeps the main effects it grows a pair from. A predictor in no set is not used. Applies together with max_interaction: set max_interaction = 0 to let the sets alone decide. NULL means no constraint. One use is to refit the forest on the effects a first fit found, e.g. after dropping its small components.

loss

[character(1) | NULL: NULL]: Loss function. NULL uses "L2" for regression, the only supported loss, and "exponential" for classification. Classification also supports "logit", which gives similar results but is slower, and "L1" and "L2", which fit class indicators directly and do not yield proper probability estimates.

delta

[numeric(1): 0.001]: Only used if loss is "logit" or "exponential". Class proportions are truncated to [delta, 1 - delta] when computing the loss of a split. Must be less than 0.5, from where every proportion is truncated to the same value, and positive for "logit": with delta = 0, nodes containing a single class have infinite loss and their splits are always rejected.

epsilon

[numeric(1): 0.1]: Only used if loss is "logit" or "exponential". Class proportions are truncated to [epsilon, 1 - epsilon] when computing the fit in a leaf. Unlike delta, this caps the size of individual leaf updates and acts as regularization: smaller values permit larger jumps on the link scale. Must be greater than 0 and less than 0.5: at 0 the leaf values of pure leaves are infinite, and from 0.5 on every leaf value is 0.

purify

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether to purify the forest after fitting, which predict_components() requires, with the defaults of purify(). For other settings, call purify() after fitting instead.

nthreads

[integer(1): 1]: Number of threads for fitting. Also the default for predict() and purify().

export_forest

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether to store the flattened forest in the returned object as $forest. If FALSE, $forest is NULL, which saves memory.

deterministic

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether to fit without randomness: no bootstrap, the first max_candidates possible splits as candidates (t_try and split_decay_rate are ignored) and evenly spaced thresholds. The result does not depend on the seed, and all tree families are identical, so use ntrees = 1. Mainly useful for testing and debugging.

keep_level_order

[logical(1) | character: FALSE]: Which factor predictors keep the order of their levels instead of being ordered by the outcome. FALSE orders every factor by the outcome, TRUE keeps the level order of every factor, and a character vector keeps it for the named factor predictors only. See "Factor predictors" below.

Value

Object of class "rpf" with model object contained in $fit.

Details

Choosing parameters

Start with max_interaction and splits. max_interaction sets which effects the model can represent: 1 for an additive model, 2 (the default) to add pairwise interactions, which can still be plotted as heatmaps. Higher values are more flexible, but slower and the components are harder to interpret. splits sets how closely the model follows the data and is the parameter to tune. With a higher max_interaction, splits are spread over more possible components, so tune both together.

ntrees averages over bootstrap samples to reduce variance and fitting and prediction time grow linearly with it. The default is lower than the usual 500 trees of a random forest because each tree family is itself a complete model, a sum of trees covering all components, rather than a single tree. Averaging therefore stops paying off sooner, usually after a few dozen families. The split search parameters (split_structure, split_try, t_try, max_candidates, split_decay_rate) trade speed for a more thorough search.

For classification, "exponential" (the default) and "logit" fit on the link scale and are transformed to probabilities, "exponential" being faster. "L1" and "L2" fit class indicators directly and their probabilities are truncated to [0, 1].

Factor predictors

Factor predictors, and character predictors, which are converted to factors, are coded as integers 1, 2, ... in an order of their levels, and splits are thresholds on these codes. A split therefore separates the levels below a cut from those above it in that order.

By default, the levels are ordered by the outcome, so that the levels most alike in the outcome are neighbours (Wright and König, 2019):

  • regression: by the mean outcome of each level;

  • binary classification: by the share of the second outcome level;

  • more than two classes: by the first principal component of the class proportions of each level (Coppersmith et al., 1999).

This applies to ordered factors too. With keep_level_order, the chosen factors are instead coded in the order of levels(), as given, ordered or not, so that every split separates neighbouring levels in that order.

The coding is stored in the fit as $factor_levels, the levels of each factor in the order of their codes. predict(), predict_components() and purify() code new data by these levels, by name, so the order of the levels in new_data does not matter.

split_structure

In each round, a t_try fraction of all possible splits (capped at max_candidates) is drawn as candidates with weights exp(-split_decay_rate * age). split_structure defines what a candidate is and how its thresholds are evaluated.

  • leaves: Split candidates are (leaf, split-dimension) pairs. For each sampled candidate, split_try thresholds are drawn uniformly without replacement from the distinct values of that predictor among the leaf's rows, leaving out the smallest and, with min_leaf_rows, those that leave fewer rows on either side (all of them if there are fewer), and evaluated to choose the best split.

  • hist: As leaves, but thresholds are drawn from boundaries of quantile bins computed once per predictor, which makes evaluating them faster on large data.

  • cur_trees_1: Split candidates are (current-tree, split-dimension) pairs. For each sampled candidate, perform split_try evaluations. Each evaluation samples a leaf from the set of valid current trees (with probability proportional to its number of available thresholds) and then uniformly samples a single threshold within that leaf.

  • cur_trees_2: Split candidates are (current-tree, split-dimension) pairs. For each sampled candidate, iterate through every valid leaf. Within each leaf, sample split_try thresholds uniformly and evaluate them.

  • res_trees: Split candidates are resulting trees. For each sampled candidate, run split_try evaluations by sampling a (split-dimension, leaf) pair from all valid pairs (with probability proportional to its number of available thresholds), then uniformly sampling one threshold within that pair.

The draw of candidates for leaves

For regression with split_structure = "leaves", the global option randomPlantedForest.exact_draw chooses how the candidates are drawn. With TRUE (the default), every possible split gets a random number in every round. With FALSE, the candidates are drawn from a Fenwick tree over the weights, kept up to date between rounds, which costs a few random numbers per candidate instead. Both draw from the same distribution, but with other random numbers, so the same seed gives another (equally good) forest. Ties between equally good candidates may go to different candidates under the two draws, so with many splits, near saturation, their fits differ in distribution, though not in accuracy. With min_leaf_rows, both leave out the same candidates: those whose leaf has no threshold with that many rows on each side. The fast draw pays off on large data with many splits. The option is read when the forest is fitted and stored in params$exact_draw; it does not affect classification or the other split structures.

options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE)

Reproducibility

With the same seed, rpf() gives the same forest on the same platform, also with more threads. Another platform can give another forest for the same seed, because the integer sampling of the C++ standard library (std::uniform_int_distribution) differs between implementations, such as libc++ and libstdc++.

References

Hiabu, M., Mammen, E., & Meyer, J. T. (2020). Random Planted Forest: a directly interpretable tree ensemble. doi:10.48550/arXiv.2012.14563

Wright, M. N. & König, I. R. (2019). Splitting on categorical predictors in random forests. PeerJ 7:e6339. doi:10.7717/peerj.6339

Coppersmith, D., Hong, S. J. & Hosking, J. R. (1999). Partitioning nominal attributes in decision trees. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 3:197–217. doi:10.1023/A:1009869804967

Examples

# Regression with formula
rpfit <- rpf(mpg ~ cyl + wt, data = mtcars)

# Regression with x and y, allowing pairwise interactions
rpfit <- rpf(x = mtcars[, c("cyl", "wt", "hp")], y = mtcars$mpg, max_interaction = 2)

# Classification
rpfit <- rpf(Species ~ ., data = iris, loss = "exponential")

# A factor that keeps its level order: splits separate neighbouring levels
cars <- mtcars
cars$gear <- factor(cars$gear, levels = c(3, 4, 5))
rpfit <- rpf(mpg ~ gear + wt, data = cars, keep_level_order = "gear")
rpfit$factor_levels
#> $gear
#> [1] "3" "4" "5"
#>
